sections.title: Taxonomy and cap
sections.text: Russula pallidospora J. Blum ex Romagn. is a brittlegill in the family Russulaceae (Basidiomycota), published in 1967 and recognized as the current name by Index Fungorum. The fleshy cap is generally 6–15 cm wide and centrally depressed even in young specimens, becoming broadly and then deeply funnel-shaped. Its thick margin remains inrolled and non-striate. The matte, finely felted cuticle is difficult to peel; it starts whitish to ivory, then often develops yellow, yellow-orange or reddish-ochre tones, especially with age or after damage.

sections.title: Gills, stem and spore print
sections.text: The gills are thick and fairly crowded, with numerous short lamellulae and some forks; they start whitish and become cream to yellowish or orange-tinged. The stem is very short, thick, firm and solid, white then sometimes yellow or brownish ochre, usually cylindrical or slightly narrowed towards the base. The flesh is firm and white, sometimes yellowing, particularly in the stem; the odour is distinctly fruity, like apple compote, and the taste is described as mild at first but sometimes bitter or acrid in the gills. The spore print is medium to dark cream (2d in the Czech Myko Atlas; medium cream IIC in Russula-Micro), darker than that of Russula delica and R. chloroides. The broadly ellipsoid spores measure about 6.5–9 × 6–7 µm in the Czech Myko Atlas; their low warts are joined by ridges, making an incomplete to nearly complete network.

sections.title: Ecology and similar species
sections.text: This rare brittlegill fruits mainly from July to October in broad-leaved woods, usually under oak and beech; records under pine are also reported. Descriptions especially associate it with calcareous soil and also mention mixed woodland. Like other Russula species, it associates with tree roots and forms ectomycorrhizae. It can be confused with Russula delica or R. chloroides, but its darker spore print, firm flesh, fruity smell and lack of blue-green gill tints help distinguish it. R. pallidospora is a separate taxon from R. subpallidospora, a newly described European species delimited by a taxonomic study published in 2025; species-level identification may require microscopic characters or molecular data.

sections.title: Caution
sections.text: The Czech Mycological Society Myko Atlas classifies this species as inedible; another specialist account also considers it unsuitable for eating because of its bitterness. Do not taste a mushroom to identify it or eat one based on a photograph or this profile.

traits: Russulaceae; Russula pallidospora J. Blum ex Romagn., published in 1967 and recognized by Index Fungorum
Fleshy cap 6–15 cm wide, depressed from a young age and later broadly funnel-shaped; matte finely felted cuticle, whitish to cream with yellow or ochre aging tones
Thick, fairly crowded gills with many lamellulae and some forks, whitish then cream to yellowish/orange-tinged
Very short, thick, firm, solid stem, white then sometimes yellow or brownish ochre; firm white flesh that may yellow
Fruity apple-compote odour; gills sometimes bitter or acrid; medium to dark cream spore print, darker than in R. delica and R. chloroides
Rare in broad-leaved woods, mainly under oak and beech, also recorded under pine; especially on calcareous soils, July to October
Classified as inedible by the Czech Myko Atlas; a photograph alone cannot establish a reliable identification
safetyNote: The Czech Mycological Society Myko Atlas classifies Russula pallidospora as inedible. Never taste or eat a russula identified from this profile or a photograph; reliable identification may require microscopic or molecular characters.
